claims.text: Homogenized equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi has a single-phase FCC microstructure.
The baseline CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a thermal conductivity of approximately 10 W/m·K at 700 °C.
The baseline CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 800 MPa.
The baseline CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 700 °C.
Adding 5 at.% Cu and aging the alloy will produce Cu-rich precipitates approximately 50–150 nm in size.
The Cu-rich precipitates will form a semi-continuous network dispersed in the FCC matrix.
Cu-rich precipitates will act as high-conductivity conduits that enhance electronic transport through the alloy.
Cu-rich precipitates will enhance phonon transport through the alloy.
The Cu-rich precipitates will not interrupt the FCC lattice continuity responsible for mechanical strength.
The intervention will increase thermal conductivity at 700 °C by approximately 20%, from about 10 to 12 W/m·K.
The intervention will reduce room-temperature yield strength by less than 5%, leaving it at or above 760 MPa.
The modified alloy will retain at least 360 MPa yield strength at 700 °C.
The modified alloy will preserve more than 90% of its room-temperature and high-temperature strength under reactor-relevant loading.
The predicted benefit will hold from 600 to 800 °C under uniaxial loading up to 80% of baseline yield strength, in inert helium and during thermal cycling between room temperature and 800 °C.
Above 800 °C, precipitate coarsening may negate the thermal or mechanical benefits.
Under oxidizing or plasma exposure, oxidation may negate the thermal or mechanical benefits.
The proposed behavior is extrapolated from Cu additions in other FCC high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and experimental design describe a 5 at.% Cu modification, whereas the stated nominal composition Cr18Mn18Fe18Co18Ni18Cu10 contains 10 at.% Cu.
The hypothesis requires retention of more than 90% of high-temperature strength, but the predicted minimum of 360 MPa relative to a 400 MPa baseline is exactly 90%, not more than 90%.

The core hypothesis requires greater than 90% high-temperature strength retention, but the falsification rule only rejects retention below 85%; results between 85% and 90% would violate the stated hypothesis without falsifying it under the specified rule.
